title: Roman Concrete Heals Its Own Cracks. Ours Can't

scenes.text: Roman concrete heals its own cracks. Ours can't.
The Pantheon's dome is almost 1,900 years old, with no steel inside, and still standing.
Experts blamed the tiny white lumps in Roman concrete on sloppy mixing. In 2023, MIT found they're the secret.
When a crack reaches a lump, rainwater dissolves it, and it recrystallizes, sealing the crack shut.
scenes.keywords: water flowing over stone close up

scenes.text: In the lab, cracked Roman-style concrete sealed itself in two weeks. The modern version never did.
Two thousand years later, we're copying them. Concrete that heals itself.

description:
Ancient Roman concrete can heal its own cracks, and modern concrete can't.
In 2023, MIT researchers led by Admir Masic showed that the small white lime clasts in Roman concrete, long dismissed as poor mixing, dissolve when water enters a crack and recrystallize as calcium carbonate, sealing it. Cracked samples healed within two weeks; a modern control never did.
Which ancient building do you think will outlast everything built today?
first_comment: The Romans also mixed volcanic ash into harbour concrete that gets stronger in seawater. Which ancient building do you think will outlast everything built today?
